topics.name: Modals of deduction (must have, can't have)
Linking words (although, despite, however, no sooner)

options: The manager asked me what I wanted.
The manager asked me what did I want.
The manager asked me that what I wanted.
questions.rule: A reported question uses statement word order and no that: asked me what I wanted.

options: I realised that I had wrote fifty-six instead of six.
I realised that I had written fifty-six instead of six.
I realised that I had writing fifty-six instead of six.
questions.rule: Past perfect = had + past participle: had written.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After had we need the past participle: had never opened.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A reported command uses told + person + to + base verb: told me to come out.
To guess about the past, use must have + past participle: must have thought.

questions.after: he was nervous, he went into the bank.
questions.rule: Although joins a full clause (he was nervous). Despite needs a noun, and however cannot join two clauses.
In a reported question the subject comes before the verb: where I kept, not where did I keep.

chat: Aman's phone is on his desk, but he isn't here.
options: He must went to the canteen.
He must have gone to the canteen.
He must have go to the canteen.
questions.rule: A guess about the past: must have + past participle: must have gone.

chat: What did the bank clerk say to you?
options: He said that my account were ready.
He said that my account was ready.
He said me that my account was ready.
questions.rule: Said takes no person after it (said me is wrong), and account is singular: was ready.

questions.source: "Can I see the manager?" I said.
options: I asked if can I see the manager.
I asked if I could see the manager.
I asked that could I see the manager.
questions.rule: A yes/no question is reported with if, statement order, and can becomes could.

options: Although his fear, he opened an account.
Despite of his fear, he opened an account.
Despite his fear, he opened an account.
questions.rule: Despite is followed directly by a noun (no of). Although needs a full clause.

options: Nobody laughed, so they can't have heard the joke.
Nobody laughed, so they can't have hear the joke.
Nobody laughed, so they can't has heard the joke.
questions.rule: To say something surely did not happen, use can't have + past participle: can't have heard.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Must have is followed by the past participle: must have left.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Despite cannot join two clauses. Use the conjunction but to show contrast: tired, but she still played.

questions.after: I was one of Pinkerton's men.
questions.rule: A reported yes/no question is joined with whether or if, never that.

questions.before: When I reached the bank, the manager
questions.rule: The leaving happened before I reached (past), so use the past perfect: had already left.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence that guesses about the past.
questions.rule: must have been shows we are sure about something in the past.

chat: Did you really go to the bank in that heavy rain?
options: Yes, despite the rain, I went.
Yes, despite it rained, I went.
Yes, although the rain, I went.
questions.rule: Despite + noun: despite the rain. Although would need a clause: although it rained.

questions.source: The clerk counted the money. He gave me a slip.
options: After the clerk had counted the money, he had give me a slip.
After the clerk has counted the money, he gave me a slip.
After the clerk had counted the money, he gave me a slip.
questions.rule: The earlier action takes the past perfect (had counted); the later one takes the simple past (gave).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: After a past reporting verb, tenses move back: has to had, want to wanted, will to would.

options: The manager ordered him that come out.
The manager ordered him to come out.
The manager ordered him to came out.
questions.rule: A command is reported with ordered/told + person + to + base verb: ordered him to come out.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After the past verb asked, the present continuous moves back: am drawing becomes was drawing.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Past perfect = had + past participle: had already started.

questions.after: have known much about banks; he even walked into the safe.
questions.rule: To say we are sure something was NOT true in the past, use can't have + past participle.
However is a linking adverb; it comes after a semicolon and is followed by a comma.
had never seen is the past perfect; size comes before material: big iron safe.

chat: What did your teacher tell you today?
options: She said us to bring our project files tomorrow.
She told us to bring our project files tomorrow.
She told us bring our project files tomorrow.
questions.rule: Use told + person + to + verb. Said cannot take a person straight after it.

chat: Is that Rohan at the door? I thought he was in Pune this week.
options: No, it can't be him; he is in Pune.
No, it can't is him; he is in Pune.
No, it can't been him; he is in Pune.
questions.rule: For a present deduction use can't + base verb: it can't be him.

questions.source: Although the manager was busy, he met me.
options: Despite the manager was busy, he met me.
Despite being busy, the manager met me.
Despite of being busy, the manager met me.
questions.rule: Despite takes a noun or an -ing form, never a full clause and never of.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Earlier past action: had closed, had forgotten (past participle). The story's next step is simple past: went.

options: He asked me if my money had been deposited.
He asked me if had my money been deposited.
He asked me if my money had deposited.
questions.rule: Money does not deposit itself, so use the passive had been deposited, in statement word order.

options: He was too nervous that he could not speak.
He was so nervous to speak.
He was so nervous that he could not speak.
questions.rule: Use so ... that or too ... to; do not mix them.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Passive deduction: must have been + past participle: must have been counted.

questions.before: The clerk asked me how I
questions.rule: Reported question: past tense after asked and statement order: how I wanted.
because joins the main clause to the clause that gives the reason.

chat: What did the manager ask you when you went in?
options: He asked me whether I was a detective.
He asked me whether was I a detective.
He asked to me whether I was a detective.
questions.rule: asked + person (no to) + whether + subject + verb: whether I was.

chat: Had you ever written a cheque before today?
options: No, I had never written one before.
No, I had never wrote one before.
No, I had not never written one before.
questions.rule: Past perfect uses the past participle written; not never is a double negative.

questions.source: "Are you drawing it all out again?" he asked in surprise.
options: He asked in surprise whether was I drawing it all out again.
He asked in surprise whether I was drawing it all out again.
He asked in surprise whether I am drawing it all out again.
questions.rule: Use whether, statement order, change you to I, and move are drawing back to was drawing.

questions.source: I am sure the clerks laughed at him.
options: The clerks must have laughed at him.
The clerks must laughed at him.
The clerks must have laugh at him.
questions.rule: I am sure + past action = must have + past participle: must have laughed.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Despite + noun, although + clause; the verb waited needs the adverb patiently.

options: The manager told the accountant that I was opening an account and would deposit fifty-six dollars.
The manager told to the accountant that I was opening an account and would deposit fifty-six dollars.
The manager said the accountant that I was opening an account and would deposit fifty-six dollars.
questions.rule: told + person directly (no to); said needs to before a person: said to the accountant.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The pair is always no sooner ... than (but hardly ... when).

questions.after: the cheque carefully, or he would not have written fifty-six instead of six.
questions.rule: After a modal, use have (never has/had) + past participle: can't have checked.
"How will you have it?" becomes how I would have the money: statement order, will to would.

chat: Why did the clerk look so surprised when he saw your cheque?
options: Because I had wrote fifty-six instead of six on it.
Because I had written fifty-six instead of six on it.
Because I have been written fifty-six instead of six on it.
questions.rule: The mistake came before his surprise, so use the past perfect with the participle: had written.

questions.source: "Let us do this painful thing quickly," I said to the clerk.
options: I suggested to the clerk that we should do that painful thing quickly.
I suggested to the clerk that let us do that painful thing quickly.
I suggested the clerk to do that painful thing quickly.
questions.rule: Let us is reported with suggested (to someone) that we should; this becomes that.

questions.source: As soon as I left the bank, the clerks burst out laughing.
options: No sooner did I left the bank than the clerks burst out laughing.
No sooner had I left the bank when the clerks burst out laughing.
No sooner had I left the bank than the clerks burst out laughing.
questions.rule: No sooner had + subject + past participle ... than + simple past.

questions.source: Mr Montgomery counted the money. Then I signed the book.
options: Mr Montgomery had counted the money before I signed the book.
Mr Montgomery had counted the money before I had sign the book.
Mr Montgomery has counted the money before I signed the book.
questions.rule: The first action takes the past perfect (had counted), the second the simple past (signed).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: must have / can't have always take the past participle: gone, walked, ridden.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: After past reporting verbs: can to could, will to would; told her to + base verb: to fill in.
